absent: Initialization and lifetime of the global timecounter pointer and host interrupt numbers and flags are not shown.
Full type definitions and sizes for timer contexts, timer maps, per cpu timer blocks, virtual cpus, guests and interrupt objects are not shown, only field uses.
Computation of timer offsets and backing system register layouts beyond identifier names is not shown.
Counterpart that loads timer state into hardware and the enable sequence for the timer block are not shown.
Behaviour of cross dossier primitives for locking, timers, reference counting, speculation hardening and diagnostics is not shown here.
VGIC distributor initialization, SPI count selection, affinity configuration and deactivation handling are not shown.
Direct injection queueing and GICv5 hardware identifier translation details are not shown.
User space interrupt chip notification transport beyond level mask computation is not shown.

findings.text: Control and compare value readers are provided for timer contexts, resolving the owning virtual cpu and choosing among virtual, physical and hyp register backings according to the timer index, with a diagnostic and a zero result for an unexpected index.

A physical counter reader exposes the host count through the global timecounter clock, and a map builder populates direct and emulated virtual and physical slots for a virtual cpu based on nested virtualization presence, hyp context and VHE support, followed by a trace carrying the virtual cpu identifier.

Injection, queueing, target selection, lookup and release operations for virtual interrupts are provided, accepting guest and virtual cpu handles plus identifiers and levels where relevant, and returning interrupt objects or status codes while managing references for LPI objects.

Helpers report whether a virtual cpu has an expired wait for timer condition and whether user space needs notification about virtual or physical timer levels, plus a run state updater that toggles the corresponding device level bits and reports if any changed.
Default private interrupt numbers are physical timer 30, virtual timer 27, hyp physical timer 26 and hyp virtual timer 28.

The count of timers considered for a virtual cpu depends on nested virtualization support, using a smaller EL0 only count when nested support is absent and a larger count covering hyp timers when present.

The flag provider for timer interrupts yields a software resample request when global VGIC state indicates no hardware deactivation and yields no flags otherwise, and two operation tables expose input level handling with either flag provision or direct injection queueing for newer VGIC.
A timer is treated as enabled when its control value carries the enable request without the mask request, and a diagnostic is expected when this check is applied to a loaded context.

Pending status for a missing context is false, for a loaded context it reflects hardware control state requiring enable plus asserted status without mask with virtual and hyp virtual sharing one system control and physical and hyp physical sharing another, and for an unloaded context it requires enabled state plus a compare value at or before physical time minus offset.
For a hyp context guest virtual or physical timer, the status bit inside the stored control value is updated to match the supplied level, leaving other timer kinds untouched.

Interrupt level updates first publish status and trace the virtual cpu and interrupt identity, then stop without injection for user space interrupt chips, and on newer VGIC stop for direct virtual or physical timers while other cases proceed to VGIC injection with the owning context as owner.

Remaining time is derived from physical time minus offset compared against a target value, converting a future difference from cycles to nanoseconds while preserving fractional remainder and yielding zero when already reached, and the earliest expiry is the minimum across enabled timers plus an active wait for timer delay, or zero when nothing can fire.

Injection is accepted only when the supplied owner matches the stored owner, with level signalling accepted on change and edge signalling accepted when the new level is asserted, and pending state is the latch for edge type versus latch or line level for level type.

Target selection keeps an active interrupt on its current or configured virtual cpu, forwards an enabled and pending interrupt to its configured target unless the distributor is disabled, and otherwise selects no target.

Shared interrupt lookup rejects newer VGIC models, maps shared peripheral identifiers into a per guest array with speculation hardening, delegates LPI identifiers to a separate lookup, and private lookup serves per virtual cpu arrays with hardware identifier translation and bounds checks for newer models before falling back to shared lookup.

Queueing honours a custom operation when installed, otherwise it resolves a target and when already assigned or without a target it releases the lock and signals the virtual cpu without insertion, else it inserts at the tail of the target list under ordered locking with retry on concurrent reassignment and requests a broadcast kick when the first active shared peripheral arrives on models needing global deactivation trapping.

Emulation publishes the current pending level and stops when pending or disabled, otherwise it arms a soft timer for the computed remaining delay, while saving is a no operation when the timer block is disabled or the context is not loaded and otherwise captures control and compare state, adjusts for offsets including a broken offset quirk, disables the hardware control and zeroes the relevant offset before clearing the loaded mark.

User notification need is computed by toggling stored device level bits against current pending states for virtual and physical timers and masking to those two timer bits, so only genuine changes in those timers request notification.

Reference handling treats non LPI interrupts as always successfully referenced without counting, while LPI interrupts use a reference count that must be non zero to acquire and whose release erases the object from the index and frees it through deferred reclamation.

Injection and queueing serialize on the per interrupt lock with interrupt state preserved, list insertion additionally takes the per virtual cpu list lock with the interrupt lock dropped and reacquired in a defined order plus retry, and LPI lifetime uses read side critical sections for lookup plus the index lock for release with an assertion that the index lock is held during erase.
State saving preserves local interrupt state across the whole capture and disable sequence, restoring it on all paths including the early exit for an unloaded context.

The timer mapping carries four context references for direct virtual, direct physical, emulated virtual and emulated physical use, where absent slots are represented by null and populated slots point at per virtual cpu timer contexts selected by mode.

Observed timer context state includes a loaded mark, a high resolution timer node and a nanosecond fraction for conversion, observed per cpu timer state includes an enabled mark, a background timer node and a timer array, and observed interrupt state includes lock, owner, configuration, line level, latch, active, enabled, target and assigned virtual cpu, list linkage, identifier, reference count and optional operations.

Background and per timer expiry handlers rearm when remaining delay is non zero to tolerate early host wakeups and otherwise complete by waking the virtual cpu or asserting the timer level, the loaded mark moves from set to cleared during save with hardware disabled, and queue insertion loops back to target resolution when concurrent assignment or affinity change is detected.

The host timer interrupt entry tolerates a null virtual cpu caused by a late interrupt after release, rebuilds the timer map, dispatches to the direct virtual or physical context based on whether the interrupt matches the host virtual line, refreshes the virtual interrupt when the context is pending, and for user space chips without active state support it disables the host virtual line.

Risks include use of stale host interrupts after virtual cpu release, early expiry from host clock adjustments requiring rearm checks, speculative index hardening for interrupt arrays, diagnostics for loaded contexts and unexpected timer indices with a fatal path for an impossible timer count, and races between queue insertion and affinity or pending changes handled by lock ordering and retry.

Soft timers are armed with an absolute hard deadline computed from current time plus the supplied nanoseconds and are cancelled through the matching cancel primitive, user space chip detection is the negation of in kernel chip presence, and broadcast kick need requires both a hardware trapping capability and a version three guest model.

Injection is a silent success when the distributor is uninitialized, rejects a missing virtual cpu for a private identifier and a missing interrupt object as invalid, and silently succeeds without state change when validation fails, otherwise it updates level or latch state before queueing and always balances the lookup reference.
Control and compare writers store supplied values into the backing system register selected by the timer index among virtual, physical and hyp variants, with a diagnostic for an unexpected index.

Module state holds a global timecounter pointer, host virtual and physical interrupt numbers with associated flag words, disabled by default feature keys for active state handling and broken offset compensation, and a fixed default PPI table indexed by timer kind.
